nodes.text: How many training rows do you have?
nodes.hint: Count of rows in your dataset after cleaning (shown in the Preview panel header).

nodes.text: Is the response expected to be smooth (no sharp jumps or discontinuities)?
nodes.hint: Physical intuition: does the output change gradually as inputs change, or are there sudden transitions (e.g. flow separation onset, buckling)?

nodes.reason: With fewer than 30 rows and a smooth response, GPR is the best choice. It uses all data efficiently, provides uncertainty estimates, and fits exactly through training points. Use Leave-One-Out CV to evaluate performance on this small dataset.

For rough responses on small datasets, use GPR with the Matérn 1.5 kernel. Matérn 1.5 is once differentiable and handles sharp curvature better than the default RBF kernel. If the response has discontinuities, consider collecting more data — fewer than 30 points is insufficient to characterise a rough response reliably.

nodes.text: How many input variables do you have?
nodes.hint: Count your designated input columns after any filtering. If you applied PCA in Step 7 — Filter, count the principal components retained, not the original column count.

nodes.text: Do you need uncertainty estimates alongside predictions?

nodes.reason: GPR is the standard choice for low-dimensional smooth responses in this size range. It provides native posterior uncertainty estimates (shown as error bars on the parity plot). Default to the RBF kernel; switch to Matérn 2.5 or 1.5 in the GPR kernel selector if the initial fit is poor.

nodes.text: Is the response smooth, or does it have non-linearities and sharp features?

nodes.reason: For smooth low-dimensional responses, GPR is excellent. Start with the default RBF kernel; if R² is below 0.90, try Matérn 2.5 using the kernel selector in the hyperparameter panel. If exact sensitivity analysis is also required, consider PCE as a fast alternative that produces Sobol indices analytically.

Random Forest handles non-smooth, discontinuous responses naturally and is robust to outliers. It will not be as accurate as GPR on a smooth response with the same data, but it degrades gracefully when the response has complex structure GPR cannot capture.

nodes.text: Is the response smooth and well-behaved?

nodes.reason: GPR remains viable up to ~15 inputs if the response is smooth. Performance degrades above 10 inputs because the kernel length-scale optimisation becomes harder. If R² < 0.90 with the default RBF kernel, try Matérn 2.5 via the kernel selector before switching model types. If R² is still low, try RF.
For 9–15 inputs with non-smooth behaviour, RF is the safer choice. It is robust to irrelevant inputs (they are rarely selected as split candidates), so high dimensionality hurts it less than GPR.

Above 15 inputs, GPR kernel optimisation becomes unreliable (curse of dimensionality) and training time grows. RF handles high-dimensional inputs robustly due to random feature subsampling and is the recommended default. If interpretability is critical, try Linear as a baseline first.

nodes.text: Random Forest (RF) — GPR not recommended above 2,000 rows
nodes.reason: GPR training scales as O(n³) — with 2,000+ rows it becomes impractically slow (minutes to hours). RF trains in seconds even on 100,000 rows. If a smooth interpolant is essential, consider downsampling to 1,500 representative points and training GPR on the reduced set.
Large datasets with non-smooth responses are RF's strongest use case. Scales efficiently, handles non-linearity naturally, and provides a useful uncertainty proxy via tree variance spread.
